passage:
Hi Kavitha,
No reply needed to this, honestly.
I've noticed you've skipped the team dinners since you joined, and when anyone asks about home you steer us back to the project. That's completely your call, and I'm not trying to dig. I just wanted to say that I walk to the tea stall by the metro at four most days. It's ten minutes, the chai is too sweet and I mostly complain about spreadsheets. If you ever feel like coming, just stand up when I do. If not, no problem at all, and I won't keep asking every day.
Also, your slides on Tuesday were really clear.
Shalini

qa.q: When does Shalini walk to the tea stall by the metro?
qa.a: At four most days.

qa.q: Why does Shalini say "No reply needed"?
qa.a: Shalini wants Kavitha to feel no pressure and is careful not to seem to be digging into Kavitha's private life.

qa.q: What makes "just stand up when I do" a good invitation?
qa.a: It lets Kavitha join without explaining or saying yes out loud, so trust can grow at Kavitha's own pace.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel reading this email?
qa.a: Kavitha might feel noticed but not cornered, and perhaps a little less alone, since the offer asks for nothing back.

grounding: A colleague notices someone who deflects personal questions and skips dinners, and offers easy company without pushing for confidences.

passage: You want to know how Hrithik and I became friends? It took most of a year. When I, Pankaj, joined the site office, he was the engineer who ate alone in the jeep. Ask him about his weekend and he'd say, "Nothing much. What about the pour schedule?" He said no to the Diwali lunch, no to cricket, no to my cousin's wedding. I didn't push. I just started buying two cups of tea at five and leaving one on his dashboard. Some days he drank it, some days it went cold. Around March he walked with me to the gate. In June he mentioned, very quickly, that his father was ill back in Nagpur. I didn't ask more than he offered. Last week he invited me to his flat for dinner. That was his idea, not mine.

qa.q: What did Pankaj leave on Hrithik's dashboard?
qa.a: A cup of tea, bought at five.

qa.q: What might Hrithik's quick mention of his ill father suggest about how he was feeling?
qa.a: He was carrying a worry he didn't usually share; saying it quickly suggests he was starting to trust Pankaj but still felt guarded.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj's choice not to ask more matter?
qa.a: It let Hrithik keep control over what he shared, so trust kept growing until the dinner invitation came from him.

qa.q: What might the months of tea have been like for Hrithik?
qa.a: They were probably a steady, quiet sign that someone cared, letting him warm up at his own pace without being put on the spot.

grounding: A colleague keeps offering low-pressure company to a co-worker who deflects and declines, and trust builds slowly at that person's pace.

passage: I'm Preeti, and I teach Class 6 English. Jagdish joined our staff room in June to teach science. I can't tell you what was going on inside him; I can only say what I saw. He kept his lunchbox shut until the rest of us had left. When Sunita ma'am asked if he was married, he laughed and said, "Married to lab reports." He skipped the staff picnic and the farewell tea. I didn't know if he was shy, sad or just private. So every Friday I asked, "Walking to the bus stop? No pressure." He said no six Fridays in a row. On the seventh he said, "Okay, today." We mostly walked in silence. Now we walk every Friday, and last week he told me about his mother's village. I still don't know everything. I don't need to.

qa.q: What did Jagdish say when asked if he was married?
qa.a: He laughed and said, "Married to lab reports."

qa.q: How did Preeti feel about not knowing what was going on inside Jagdish?
qa.a: Preeti felt unsure whether he was shy, sad or just private, so she kept offering the Friday walk with no pressure. She is content not to know everything.

qa.q: What choice did Preeti make after six refusals, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Preeti kept asking calmly each Friday without pushing or taking offence, so Jagdish could join when he was ready 🙂

qa.q: Why might Jagdish have kept his lunchbox shut until the others left?
qa.a: He may have wanted privacy or felt shy about questions; the passage leaves it open, just as Preeti does.

grounding: A colleague notices a new teacher who deflects questions and skips gatherings, and keeps offering easy company until he joins in his own time.

passage:
Monday. Sunaina noticed that Vikas, the new analyst on her floor, answered every "How was your weekend?" with "Fine. Did the report go out?" He turned down the Friday team lunch too. She didn't push.
Thursday. At four she stopped by his desk with two cups from the machine. "Taking a tea break. Want one? No need to talk." He hesitated, took it, and they stood by the window. He said nothing about himself. She talked about the traffic.
Three weeks later. The tea breaks had become a habit, three times a week. One afternoon, without her asking, Vikas said his father had been unwell and he had moved to the city alone. Sunaina just listened, then said, "Same time tomorrow?" He nodded. "Same time."

qa.q: What did Vikas answer when asked about his weekend?
qa.a: He answered, 'Fine. Did the report go out?'

qa.q: What might Vikas have been feeling when he hesitated before taking the tea?
qa.a: He may have felt unsure and guarded, wary that accepting would lead to personal questions.

qa.q: What did Sunaina do that let trust grow at Vikas's pace?
qa.a: She offered tea with no need to talk, kept showing up, and only listened when he chose to share about his father.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel when Vikas finally tells her about his father?
qa.a: Sunaina may feel glad and trusted, since her patient tea breaks let him open up without being asked, and she keeps the habit going.

grounding: Over three weeks a colleague notices a new analyst who deflects personal questions and keeps offering low-pressure tea, letting trust build at his pace.

passage:
"Maria, you asked what to do about the quiet new girl in your office. Let me, your old Dilnaz, tell you about Rosamma.
I was twenty-five, a clerk at the Byculla post office. Rosamma had come from Kerala, sorted mail beside me and said almost nothing. If I asked about her family, she'd say, 'All fine,' and ask about the stamps. She never came for the Friday samosas.
I didn't dig. I just started saying, 'I'm walking to the bus stop, come if you like.' Most days she didn't. Some days she did, and we walked without talking.
After four months, on one of those walks, she told me her mother had died that year and she had no one in the city. I only listened. We were friends for forty years, Maria. Offer the walk. Let her decide when."

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz work at twenty-five?
qa.a: Dilnaz was a clerk at the Byculla post office.

qa.q: Why do you think Dilnaz chose not to dig into Rosamma's family?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt patient and a little protective, sensing Rosamma wasn't ready and worried that pressing would only push Rosamma further away.

qa.q: What small offer did Dilnaz keep making, and why did it work?
qa.a: Dilnaz kept inviting Rosamma to walk to the bus stop, which was easy to refuse and let trust build until Rosamma chose to share.

qa.q: What might those quiet walks have meant to Rosamma?
qa.a: They may have given her company without questions at a lonely time, after losing her mother far from home. 🤍

grounding: An elder recalls noticing a withdrawn colleague and offering low-pressure walks, letting trust build at the colleague's own pace.

passage: With the audit due Friday and half the team out sick, the Nagpur office was all ringing phones and cold chai. Irfan noticed Tanuja again: headphones on, lunch at her desk, a quick "all good!" whenever anyone asked about her weekend. She'd said no to the team dinner, the cricket match, the farewell. Irfan didn't push. On Tuesday he left a cutting chai beside her keyboard and said, "Going to the tapri at four if you want a break. No pressure." She didn't come. Wednesday, same. Thursday, at four-fifteen, she appeared at the tapri, arms crossed against the wind. They talked about the audit for ten minutes, nothing personal. As they walked back, Tanuja said, "Thanks for not asking stuff." Irfan just nodded. He planned to go again at four next week.

qa.q: What did Irfan leave beside Tanuja's keyboard on Tuesday?
qa.a: He left a cutting chai beside her keyboard.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling as he kept inviting Tanuja despite her silence?
qa.a: Irfan seemed quietly concerned for Tanuja and patient, not hurt by her refusals, which is why he kept the offer light.

qa.q: Why does Irfan's approach suit someone like Tanuja?
qa.a: Low-pressure invitations with no personal questions let Tanuja come on her own terms, so trust can build at her pace.

qa.q: What does Tanuja's "Thanks for not asking stuff" reveal about her experience?
qa.a: It suggests Tanuja often feels pressed to explain herself and was relieved to have company that asked for nothing.

grounding: A colleague notices someone deflecting personal questions and declining invitations, and keeps offering low-pressure tea so trust builds at her pace.

passage: Aniket had worked beside Gurleen at the Kolkata design studio for four months and still knew nothing about her beyond her coffee order. Ask about her weekend and she'd say "quiet," then ask about his. She skipped every birthday cake in the pantry. Aniket noticed she ate lunch on the fire-escape steps, alone. He didn't want to be the colleague who pries. So on Monday he said, "I walk to the lake after lunch. Join if you like, or don't." For two weeks she didn't. Then one grey Thursday she caught up with him at the gate. They walked around the lake in near-silence, watching a man feed the ducks. On the way back Gurleen said, "My mother's been unwell. I don't really talk about it." Aniket said, "Okay. Walk's there anytime." He didn't ask more.

qa.q: Where did Gurleen eat lunch?
qa.a: Gurleen ate lunch on the fire-escape steps, alone.

qa.q: What does Aniket's decision not to pry suggest he is thinking?
qa.a: Aniket seems caring but cautious, worried that pushing questions would make Gurleen withdraw further.

qa.q: How could Aniket keep supporting Gurleen after she mentioned her mother?
qa.a: He could keep offering the walk without probing, and simply listen if she brings it up again, letting her decide how much to share.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Gurleen to finally join the walk?
qa.a: It may have felt risky but relieving for Gurleen to have quiet company that didn't demand answers, enough to share one true thing.

grounding: A colleague notices someone who deflects and declines invitations, keeps offering a low-pressure walk, and lets trust build at her pace.

passage:
"Samosa?" Dilnaz held out the paper plate at the office pantry.
"No, thanks. Ate already," Mahima said, eyes on her phone.
"Okay." Dilnaz sat on the other stool anyway. "I'm going down to the bakery tomorrow at five. Their chai's terrible. You're welcome to suffer with me."
"Maybe. I've got a lot on."
"No problem."
Next day, five o'clock. Dilnaz knocked on Mahima's cabin door. "Bakery. Still terrible. Still going."
Mahima hesitated. "I really can't today."
"Sure. Same time Friday."
Friday, Mahima was already standing by the lift, bag on her shoulder. "Is it really that bad?"
"Worse," Dilnaz grinned.
Over the cracked cups, Mahima said, "I moved here after a break-up. I don't really know anyone."
Dilnaz nodded. "Well. You know the bakery now." Neither said more, and that seemed fine.

qa.q: What time does Dilnaz go to the bakery?
qa.a: Dilnaz goes to the bakery at five.

qa.q: Why does Dilnaz keep inviting Mahima after being turned down?
qa.a: Dilnaz seems to care about Mahima's loneliness and is patient, hopeful that a light, repeated offer will feel safe enough to accept.

qa.q: Which of Dilnaz's choices worked best, and why?
qa.a: Accepting each no with "No problem" and repeating the same easy invite kept pressure low, so Mahima could choose to come when she was ready.

qa.q: What would change if Dilnaz had asked Mahima directly why she was so quiet?
qa.a: Mahima might have felt cornered and closed up, and may not have shared about her move and break-up on her own.

grounding: A colleague notices someone who turns down invitations and keeps offering low-pressure company, letting trust build at her pace.

passage:
I'm Salma. I've worked beside Vasudha at the bank for a year, and I still know almost nothing about her. Whenever anyone asks about her weekend, she smiles and says, "Nothing much. And you?" She turns down every team lunch.
At first I thought she was just shy. Then I noticed her eating alone in the stairwell, and her eyes when we planned the Diwali party.
I didn't push. I just started asking, "I'm getting chai at four. Want to come?" She said no six times. The seventh time, she came. We didn't talk about anything personal. Just the rain.
Now she comes most days. Last week she mentioned her mother lives far away. It was a small thing. I didn't ask more.

qa.q: Where did Salma notice Vasudha eating?
qa.a: She noticed her eating alone in the stairwell.

qa.q: Why did Salma keep inviting Vasudha to chai without pushing?
qa.a: Salma felt concerned that Vasudha might be lonely, but wanted her to feel safe and not pressured.

qa.q: What makes Salma's approach respectful?
qa.a: She offers low-pressure company again and again, doesn't force personal talk, and lets trust grow at Vasudha's pace.

qa.q: What might it be like for Vasudha when she finally joins for chai?
qa.a: She probably feels a little nervous but relieved to have easy company without being questioned.

grounding: A colleague notices someone who deflects personal questions and eats alone, and keeps offering low-pressure chai so trust can build.

passage:
Team lead's note, design studio, Bengaluru

Avni joined our team six months ago. She's good at her work, but she deflects every personal question with a joke and has turned down every team dinner.
Vidya, a senior designer, noticed too. I watched Vidya handle it well. She didn't corner Avni or ask why. She just said, every Friday, "I'm walking to the lake at lunch, if you want company."
For weeks Avni said no. Then one Friday she came. Vidya told me they only talked about fonts and ducks.
Last week Avni stayed late to help Vidya with a deadline and mentioned she'd moved here alone after a breakup. Vidya just listened.
I'm glad we didn't push. Trust is coming.

qa.q: Where did Vidya invite Avni to walk?
qa.a: To the lake at lunch.

qa.q: What did Vidya seem to feel about Avni's distance?
qa.a: Vidya seemed concerned and patient, sensing Avni might be lonely but not wanting to pressure her.

qa.q: What made Vidya's invitations work?
qa.a: They were regular, low-pressure and without questions, letting Avni join at her own pace.

qa.q: How might Avni have felt when she mentioned the breakup?
qa.a: Avni probably felt a little vulnerable but safe enough, since Vidya had never pushed her.

grounding: A team lead describes a colleague noticing someone who deflects personal questions and offering low-pressure walks so trust can build.

passage:
Diary, Friday

Maria has worked at the next desk for four months now. She's friendly, but every time someone asks about her life, she changes the subject. She's said no to every drinks night.
I, Mridul, used to think she didn't like us. But today I saw her sitting alone in the park at lunch, feeding pigeons, looking very far away.
I didn't want to push. So I just said, on the way back, "I'm getting samosas at five. Want one?"
She hesitated. Then said yes.
We ate them standing by the tea stall and talked about nothing. She laughed at my bad joke. It's small. But I think I'll ask again on Monday. No questions, just samosas.

qa.q: What was Maria doing alone in the park?
qa.a: She was feeding pigeons, looking very far away.

qa.q: What did Mridul feel on seeing Maria alone in the park?
qa.a: Mridul felt concerned that she might be lonely, and wanted to reach out without pushing.

qa.q: What small step did Mridul plan, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To ask again on Monday with no questions, just samosas, so Maria can build trust at her own pace.

qa.q: How might Maria have felt when she laughed at the bad joke?
qa.a: She may have felt a little more relaxed and less alone.

grounding: A colleague notices someone who deflects personal questions and eats alone, and offers low-pressure company so trust can build.

passage: In the London accounts office, Tariq noticed that Kofi always ate lunch at his desk, headphones on, and answered 'Fine, thanks' to every question about his weekend. He had turned down the Friday pub three times and the team curry twice. Tariq, who didn't drink either, didn't ask why. One grey Tuesday he just stopped by Kofi's desk. 'I'm walking round the park to get a coffee. Ten minutes. Want one?' 'I'm alright, thanks.' 'No problem.' Tariq asked again on Thursday, and the next Tuesday. On the fourth try Kofi pulled off his headphones. 'Is the coffee place any good?' They walked round the pond. Kofi said little. Tariq didn't fill the silence. At the door, Kofi said, 'Same time Thursday?' as if it were nothing. Tariq nodded as if it were nothing too.

qa.a: At his desk, headphones on.

qa.q: Why didn't Tariq ask Kofi why he turned down the pub?
qa.a: Tariq felt respectful and understanding, perhaps because he didn't drink either, and didn't want Kofi to feel pressured.

qa.q: What made Tariq's invitations low-pressure?
qa.a: They were short and simple, a ten-minute coffee walk, and he accepted each no without fuss and didn't fill the silences.

qa.q: What might 'Same time Thursday?' mean for Kofi?
qa.a: It suggests Kofi is beginning to trust Tariq and wants the company, even if he says it lightly.
